messages.subject: Repeated phenotype
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I want to perform a QTL analysis of a phenotype, analyzed twice in different places and different times. In such data, not all individuals overlap between both experiments, and some of which that overlap have shown different results between these two experiments. Single QTL analysis shows several QTLs, but neither of them mapped in the same locus. I wonder if there are way to combine the data to analyze this phenotype at the same time in order to increase the confidence.
Thanks in advance

messages.subject: Re: Repeated phenotype
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I think you could either do a meta-analysis or use the program MAPQTL, which can combine data for a single phenotype if you have an integrated map from the two sets of data.

For both of these strategies the individuals you would consider should be different. That is, the two sets should not include any common individual(s). The individuals should have been generated independently by different crosses.

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Recombination Fractions >> 0.5
messages.body_plain:
It doesn't sound like a sampling error problem. Usually, when you're getting rf >> 0.5, the problem is that the genotypes that you thought were AA are really BB and vice versa.

karl

> On Sep 29, 2015, at 9:38 AM, Jim <jspe...@unl.edu> wrote:
>
> Karl & other R/qtl discussion group members:  .
>
> GBS was used to generate SNP markers for a soybean F4-derived RIL population of 211 individuals using the sequenced soybean genome (20 chrs) as the reference in Tassel for outputting a R/qtl ready data set.
>
> The *.bmp attachment shows the physical (bp) map locations of the outputted SNPs.  Obviously, there are soy chr regions (gaps) where the mated parents are monomorphic.
>
> However, the problem that prompted this (my) e-mail is when the est.rf and est.map functions were used to derive a genetic map (kosambi cM) .
>
> Many rf values for SNP pairs GREATLY exceed the theoretical expectation of 0.5 (see attached *.bmp file of LOD vs rf).  There is apparently a lot of corrective work that must be done to get this populations plot of LOD vs rf to the kind shown in Karl's Figure 10 (see attached *.bmp file) in his Guide to Mapping... tutorial).
>
> So my first question is this:  Is it common for GBS to generate a large number of SNPs in which the parental allele phase inversed (assuming that this is the cause of the rf values greater than the theoretical max of 0.5?
>
> SNP pairs with rf >>> 0.5 are not a problem so long as the SNP Pair Members are on different chromosome.  However, it is (a big) problem when the SNP pair members are on the SAME chromosome.  Indeed, when rf values for the SNP pairs on a given chr are much greater than 0.4999....  the chr cM map inflation can be huge - see *.bmp file with this population's genetic map).
>
> I recognize that sampling error occurs when one is estimating rf values for any given RIL population, even when the true SNP pair rf value is close to theoretical max pf 0.5, but rf estimates excessively greater than 0.5 translate into huge cM distances.
>
> So my second question is this:  Can one somehow restrict same chromosome SNP pairs to a max of (say) 0.4999999 to resolve this sampling error problem when rf values are converted to (kosambi) map function cM distances?
>
> If the answer to that 2nd question is NO, then I have a third question:
>
> Is there a convenient R/qtl code that can be used to EXTRACT  from the all possible SNP pair rf matrix JUST THOSE SNPs that are:
> (1) ONLY on a given specified chromosome, AND THEN (not and/or)
> (2) ONLY same-specified chromosome SNP pairs that have rf values > 0.4999.
>
> If there are a lot of SNPs that need corrective work (as Karl notes in his Guide tutorial) then I really need a short list of SNPs to get started on that work!  Any suggested short-cut R/qtl code to get the corrective work done quicker would also be greatly appreciated.
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Because you have measured the same (but not all) individuals in the two environments/times, I think you should be fitting a mixed effects model, to account for the within-individual correlation. However, unfortunately, R/qtl doesn't have any functions for this.

> Thank you very much for this hint. I even read your book in hard copy, but missed this for my problem now. But the question about the big difference with mr and em is still not totally clear for me.

See the bottom of page 79: "The jagged appearance of the LOD curve for chromosome 4 is due to the pattern of missing marker genotype data. Recall that in the marker regression method, we split the individuals into groups according to their genotype at a marker. If an individual’s genotype is missing, that individual must be omitted, as we do not know the genotype group in which it should be placed."

> And in addition, is there a way to see, if this significant interval (given this nice significant signal) is a false positive? Is there a calculation to check this?

This is what the permutation test is for. Aside from that, there's no way to know.

karl

messages.body_plain:
> Sorry for posting 2 posts directly at one time. But i forgot one question. what are the best setting in calc.genoprob for step and error? Or how can I decide on my own what to set there? Does it depend on crossing sheme, marker density?

A smaller step will mean subsequent calculations are on a tighter grid. But everything will be slower and results will take up more space.

error.prob is the assumed genotyping error rate; choice depends on your particular data. You can, in principle, estimate it (see pg 36 of http://rqtl.org/tutorials/geneticmaps.pdf). You can think of it as smoothing out the LOD curves; a larger value results in more smoothing.

karl

messages.subject: Re: Repeated phenotype
messages.body_plain:
Have you analysing your data using, e.g. REML, to partition into variance components?  You could add occasion to your experimental design and get weighted line means to use as input for the qtl analysis.  Also check to see the normality of your data before you analyses it (it may need to be transformed).  if the individuals differ greatly in phenotype score across environments then this may hint that the trait has a strong environmental component - and low heritability.  Therefor if you do three mapping exercises, 1. exp1; 2. exp2; 3 across exps and illustrate all qtls on the same linkage map you can look at which qtl differ between occasions and which if any are robust across occasions.  i agree with the previous comments.

Ah, I see!  I was confused because my plan was to use scanone and scantwo to find QTL that I would put into my makeqtl model.  Since I have multiple QTL on some chromosomes, I was hoping to include them in the model.

So, I should just incorporate the highest peak for each chromosome?  What about in the event that two peaks on the same chromosome are higher and account for more variance than the highest peak on a separate chromosome?  As an example, if I have two distinct peaks on chromosome 3 with each having a LOD score of 7 or more and another, single peak on chromosome 5 at 3.4, then is it still correct to only include the highest peak from each chromosome?

I hope I've explained my confusion accurately.  If not, please let me know.  Thank you!

Miranda

I am still a bit confused, though. My plan was to use scanone and scantwo to find QTL that I would put into my model using makeqtl and fitqtl.  The two sources you gave appear to only use the highest LOD score on each chromosome. Since I have multiple QTL on some chromosomes, I was hoping to include them in the model.

So, I should just incorporate the highest peak for each chromosome?  What about in the event that two peaks on the same chromosome are higher and account for more variance than the highest peak on a separate chromosome?  As an example, if I have two distinct peaks on chromosome 3 with each having a LOD score of 7 or more and another, single peak on chromosome 5 at 3.4, then is it still correct to only include the highest peak from each chromosome?

I have also read the MQM Tutorial <http://www.rqtl.org/tutorials/MQM-tour.pdf> which uses the locus on each chromosome with the greatest LOD score as a co-factor, but I am interested in the original LOD scores.  Using a marker as a co-factor alters the LOD score in the new analysis.

I hope I've explained my confusion accurately.  If not, please let me know.  I'm really just looking for a list of all QTL above a given threshold. Correct me if I am wrong, but I think I can do it manually for my population with 69 markers, find the marker at each cM position, and then finding the confidence interval should also give me the LOD Score at that marker.  I do not think I could do this manually with my sub-population with 578 markers, though.

Thank you!

messages.subject: Q re covariates and sex chromosome
messages.subject_clean: Q re covariates and sex chromosome
messages.body_plain:
I received the following email and thought it and my response may be of broader interest.

> I’m working on a project to identify QTL in a hybrid cross between two plant species with heteromorphic sex chromosomes and sexual dimorphism.  Currently I’m using your R/qtl pakage to run my analysis but I have a couple of questions.
>
> My study systems consist on a CP cross, with the presence of sex chromosomes and sexual dimorphism. I have 314 individuals and 655 SNP markers distributed in 12 linkage groups.
>
> As a first approach I’m running single QTL scans with the interval mapping “em” to detect for plausible QTLs and then I’m running the multiple QTL model comparison to estimate the LOD and PVE values and the possible interaction between QTLs. However, because my plants are sexually dimorphic I have biological reasons to include sex as a covariate and also to test for for the interaction between this covariable and the QTLs. The question will be:  when is the best time to include the covariable interaction, on the first interval mapping scan or just in the model comparison?
> When I run the scan just with the cov=sex (after estimating the thresholds) I end up with more QTLs than when I include cov=sex plus intcov=sex.  I find less stringent the first approach and I can refine it with the model comparison, but I’m not sure what will be the difference. For some traits it makes a huge difference, between finding 2 QTLs with no interaction to  6 QTLs  with a lot of interactions.
>
> The second question will be how is the program dealing with defining a sex chromosome and using sex as a covariate compared to when you don’t have a define sex chromosome and adding sex as a covariate. Because our sex chromosomes are still recombining a lot we explore the two possibilities and the QTLs that where significant with no sex chromosomes and sex as covariate, are not significant anymore when you have both: define sex chromosome and sex as covariate, and we are not very sure why.

There's discussion of the treatment of covariates in chapter 7 of the R/qtl book (http://www.rqtl.org/book).

If I know there's a sex difference in the phenotype, I'll always include sex as an additive covariate.

Including sex as an interactive covariate can be useful if there are QTL with big sex differences in their effect. In there are no such QTL x sex interactions, it's better to keep it as a strictly additive covariate, as the use of the interactive covariate will hurt your power to detect QTL.

Regarding sex chromosomes, R/qtl only handles the mammalian situation, of an X and a Y chromosome, with no recombination in the heterogametic sex.

I've dealt with cases where there was a sex "locus"; it seemed best to just treat it as an autosome, but to be sure to include sex as an additive covariate.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Except in large crosses, it is usually difficult to obtain good evidence for linked QTL, but I feel it's better to focus on multiple-QTL models than to look at peaks in the scanone results.

The results of scantwo can be quite informative about the possibility of two QTL on a chromosome, and scantwo will give an estimate of the locations of the two QTL, which you can then use in makeqtl() and fitqtl() for exploring larger models. It's up to you whether you want to pick out the single highest peak on a chromosome, or two pick out two peaks on the same chromosome.

You could also form a model containing the loci with major effect and then use addqtl() or addpair() to do a scan for an additional QTL or an additional pair of QTL.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I was working on the 4K GBS markers to construct genetic map of a F7 population. These 4k markers were the most confident markers in our data and they were ordered by physical position.

After removing the suspect and redundant markers, the 1K remaining markers were used to construct genetic map and I found the total map distance were quite different when I treated data as “bcsft” (F.gen=7) and “riself”.

The total map distance is about 960cM and 1820cM when I treated data as “bcsft” (F.gen=7) and “riself”, respectively. And I also found if I treat data as “f2”, I will get 1820cM just like treat it as ”riself”.

Here is my code and genetic map:

rils1=read.cross(file = "markers (delete suspect).csv" ,error.prob = 0.001,  genotypes = c("A","H","B"), alleles = c("A","B"), estimate.map = T , F.gen = 7, map.function = "kosambi")

rils2=read.cross(file = "markers (delete suspect).csv" ,error.prob = 0.001,  genotypes = c("A","H","B"), alleles = c("A","B"), estimate.map = T , crosstype = "riself", map.function = "kosambi")

rils3=read.cross(file = "markers (delete suspect).csv" ,error.prob = 0.001,  genotypes = c("A","H","B"), alleles = c("A","B"), estimate.map = T , crosstype = "f2", map.function = "kosambi")

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Warning Message: Didn't converge!
messages.body_plain:
The estimation of inter-marker distances uses an iterative algorithm, in which the estimates are gradually improved over many small steps. The algorithm is halted when the maximum absolute difference in the recombination fractions is less than "tol" (default 10^-6), in which case we say the estimates "converged"; it is alternatively halted if the number of iterations reaches "maxit" (default 10000), in which case a warning message is printed.

I would generally repeat the call to est.map(), starting at the new map. You might also increase the value of "maxit". Here's an example:

library(qtl)
data(hyper)
newmap <- est.map(hyper, err=0.01)
hyper_newmap <- replacemap(hyper, newmap)
newmap2 <- est.map(hyper_newmap, err=0.01, maxit=100000)

You might also make the "tol" value less stringent (say 10^-4) so that the algorithm meets the convergence criterion in a small number of iterations. But doing this, or ignoring the warning message, will mean that the estimated map will be not as good as it could be. But the difference may not matter.

Missing genotype data really slows down the estimation of the genetic map. I've found it sometimes useful to get an initial estimate the map using filled-in genotypes and then refine that using the actual data, something like this:

library(qtl)
data(hyper)
hyper_filled <- fill.geno(hyper)
initmap <- est.map(hyper_filled)
hyper <- replacemap(hyper, initmap)
newmap <- est.map(hyper, err=0.01)

karl
